While he doesn’t want to call AI a bubble, he notes that there has been an almost unprecedented level of investment in AI. “In the Fed world, the bigger the hype, the more nervous I am that we’re going to overheat what the economy is capable of in the next six months,” Goolsbee says. That makes consumer sentiment less critical for central bankers as they weigh the direction of the economy while deciding on the path of interest rates, he says. (Dean Seal, dean.seal@wsj.com)

Capitol Hill’s Bark Is Worse Than Its Bite for Bank Stocks
 
Plus, young entrepreneurs and a Wall Street turf war
 
 
KEVIN DIETSCH/GETTY IMAGES
 

Banks and their top executives may be in for some rough politics as Democrats sweep into power in Congress. But control of the White House is what counts most for investors.

 

Democratic leaders such as Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Sherrod Brown, who retook his Senate seat in Ohio, have been among big banks’ most vocal critics since the 2008 financial crisis. And if affordability tops the new political agenda, many bank products, from credit cards to savings accounts, will certainly come under scrutiny.

 

Yet so far, bank stocks have been spared the market’s worst fears.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

 
 
 

Planning & Investing

 

20-Somethings Are Ditching Entry-Level Jobs to Become Their Own Bosses

 

AI is shaking up the employment market for younger workers—and making it easier for them to become entrepreneurs.

 
 
 

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

The massive data center buildout spree poses some overheating risks to the economy, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee says in a Q&A at a Chicago event. He compares the recent AI boom to the dot-com bubble around 2000, and warns that lofty growth expectations can lead to disappointment. While he doesn’t want to call AI a bubble, he notes that there has been an almost unprecedented level of investment in AI. “In the Fed world, the bigger the hype, the more nervous I am that we’re going to overheat what the economy is capable of in the next six months,” Goolsbee says. (Dean Seal, dean.seal@wsj.com)

 

Readings of consumer sentiment are broadly important, just not directly applicable to the Federal Reserve’s job, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee says during a Q&A at a Chicago event. Consumer sentiment has long been a leading indicator for consumer spending, but those two data sets have broken away from each other in the past five years, he says. “Consumer sentiment has been in the toilet for now a long time,” while consumer spending has been the main driver of economic growth, Goolsbee says. That makes consumer sentiment less critical for central bankers as they weigh the direction of the economy while deciding on the path of interest rates, he says. (Dean Seal, dean.seal@wsj.com)
